levels.title: You
levels.subtitle: The center of your entire universe.
facts: Atom Count: Your body is composed of approximately 7 octillion atoms (mostly hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, and nitrogen).
Stellar Origin: Every heavier atom in your body (iron, calcium, phosphorus) was forged inside ancient dying stars billions of years ago.
Bio-Electricity: Your nervous system generates about 20 watts of electrical power—enough to dimly power a small LED light bulb.
Cellular Turnover: Every day, your body produces around 300 billion new cells to replace dead or damaged tissue.
Solar Neutrinos: Trillions of invisible neutrinos streaming from the Sun pass through your body every second without stopping.
DNA Stretch: If you uncoiled all the DNA inside your body's cells, it would stretch from the Earth to Pluto and back.
Thermal Glow: Your body radiates heat in the infrared spectrum; if our eyes could see infrared, you would glow in total darkness.
Interstellar Water: Over 60% of your body is water, much of which originated in deep interstellar molecular clouds before the solar system formed.

levels.title: Your World
levels.subtitle: Your entire existence, cradled in blue.
levels.sizeFact: Immediate Horizon: At 10 kilometers across, this represents your daily physical footprint and immediate atmospheric sphere.
Troposphere: Within this scale lies the troposphere, containing 75% of Earth's atmospheric mass and virtually all weather systems.
Human Perspective: Throughout 99% of human history, an individual's entire known world fit entirely within this single scale stop.
Sound Barrier: Sound travels across this 10km horizon in about 30 seconds under normal atmospheric conditions.
Visual Curvature: From the top of this scale, the subtle curvature of the Earth begins to become faintly perceptible.
Atmospheric Pressure: Air pressure drops by half roughly every 5.5 kilometers you ascend within this boundary.

levels.title: Earth
A pale blue speck suspended in a sunbeam.
levels.sizeFact: Sunlight takes 8 min 20 s to arrive
Orbital Velocity: Earth races around the Sun at an astonishing 107,000 km/h while spinning at 1,670 km/h at the equator.
Water vs Mass: 71% of Earth's surface is covered in water, yet water accounts for less than 0.02% of Earth's total planetary mass.
Protective Shield: Earth's molten iron outer core generates a powerful magnetosphere that deflects lethal solar wind and cosmic radiation.
Atmospheric Thinness: If Earth were the size of a basketball, its entire life-sustaining atmosphere would be thinner than a single sheet of paper.
Continental Drift: Earth's continents drift apart at about 2.5 centimeters per year—roughly the same speed as human fingernails grow.
Oblique Tilt: Earth's 23.5-degree axial tilt creates our changing seasons, stabilized permanently by our large Moon.
Ancient Atmosphere: Earth's early atmosphere had zero oxygen; it was transformed 2.4 billion years ago by photosynthetic microbes (the Great Oxidation Event).
Magnetic Poles: Earth's magnetic north and south poles wander continuously and have flipped entirely hundreds of times in geological history.

title: The Moon
Our silent neighbor, watching over our brief history.
sizeFact: 384,400 km away · Light takes 1.3 s
Tidal Locking: The Moon is tidally locked to Earth, rotating on its axis in the exact same time it takes to orbit Earth, keeping one face permanently hidden.
Drifting Away: Due to tidal friction, the Moon is slowly spiraling away from Earth at a rate of 3.8 centimeters every single year.
Impact Archive: The Moon has no atmosphere or tectonic activity, preserving impact craters from asteroid strikes spanning 4.5 billion years.
Stabilizing Axis: The Moon's gravitational pull stabilizes Earth's axial tilt, preventing extreme, chaotic climate swings.
Footprints Forever: Neil Armstrong's footprints on the lunar surface will remain undisturbed for millions of years due to the absence of wind or rain.
Moonquakes: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded moonquakes caused by Earth's gravitational tidal stress deep inside the lunar interior.
Extreme Temperatures: Lunar surface temperatures swing wildly from 127°C in direct sunlight to -173°C in permanent polar shadows.
Giant Impact: The Moon was born 4.5 billion years ago when a Mars-sized protoplanet named Theia collided with the young Earth.

title: The Sun
Our raging nuclear furnace fueling every breath you take.
sizeFact: 1.39 million km across
Solar Mass: The Sun accounts for 99.86% of all physical mass in the entire solar system.
Nuclear Fusion: Every second, the core fuses 600 million tons of hydrogen into helium, converting 4 million tons of matter directly into pure radiant energy.
Blazing Core: Temperatures at the solar core reach a staggering 15 million°C, while the visible surface (photosphere) is a relatively cool 5,500°C.
Light Travel: A photon generated at the solar core takes upwards of 100,000 years to reach the surface, but only 8 minutes to travel from the surface to Earth.
Sunspot Cycles: Every 11 years, the Sun undergoes magnetic polarity reversals, triggering intense solar flares and auroral storms on Earth.
Stellar Classification: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence star) currently halfway through its stable 10-billion-year lifespan.
Gravity Anchor: Solar gravity reaches far beyond Pluto, holding distant comets in the icy Oort Cloud.
Sound Waves: The Sun hums with standing acoustic pressure waves ringing like a giant bell, vibrating through its plasma interior.

title: Our Solar System
8 worlds dancing in the void. V1 & V2 blink back from the dark.
sizeFact: Voyager 1 & 2: 23 light-hours deep in interstellar space
Oort Cloud: The solar system's gravitational boundary extends outward into the Oort Cloud, nearly 2 light-years (halfway to Proxima Centauri).
Voyager Legacy: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is humanity's most distant emissary, transmitting data from beyond the heliosphere over 24 billion km away.
Orbital Plane: All eight planets orbit the Sun in nearly the exact same flat plane, a relic of the spinning protoplanetary disk formed 4.6 billion years ago.
Gas Giants: Jupiter and Saturn contain more than 90% of the planetary mass orbiting the Sun.
Kuiper Belt: Beyond Neptune lies a vast ring of icy primordial debris, home to dwarf planets like Pluto and Haumea.
Asteroid Belt: Located between Mars and Jupiter, the asteroid belt contains millions of rocky bodies holding clues to planet formation.
Heliosphere: The Sun creates a giant magnetic bubble called the heliosphere that shields the inner planets from galactic cosmic rays.
Planetary Migration: Evidence suggests giant planets like Jupiter and Saturn shifted dramatically in their orbits during the solar system's chaotic youth.

title: The Milky Way
400 billion stars. You are invisible from here.
exponent: 100,000 light-years across
Stellar Empire: The Milky Way contains between 100 to 400 billion stars and at least 100 billion planets.
Supermassive Heart: At the galactic center lies Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole weighing 4 million times the mass of our Sun.
Galactic Year: Our solar system takes roughly 230 million years to complete one single orbit around the galactic center (a 'galactic year').
Dark Matter Halo: Over 90% of the Milky Way's mass is invisible dark matter holding the spinning disc together against centrifugal disruption.
Stellar Cannibalism: The Milky Way has absorbed dozens of smaller satellite dwarf galaxies over its 13.6-billion-year history.
Spiral Structure: Our galaxy is a barred spiral with four major luminous arms where active star formation constantly takes place.
High-Speed Travel: The solar system orbits the galactic center at a blistering speed of 828,000 km/h.
X-Ray Bubbles: Colossal gamma-ray and X-ray bubbles extend thousands of light-years above and below the galactic plane from past black hole outbursts.

title: Our Galactic Neighborhood
A tiny cluster of island universes drifting in nothingness.
exponent: 10 million light-years across
Local Group: Our galaxy is part of the Local Group—a gravitational club of over 80 galaxies spanning 10 million light-years.
Andromeda Collision: The Milky Way and the neighboring Andromeda Galaxy are hurtling toward each other at 110 km/s, scheduled to merge in ~4.5 billion years.
Dwarf Companions: The Local Group is dominated by giant spirals (Milky Way and Andromeda) accompanied by dozens of tiny dwarf spheroidal galaxies.
Triangulum Galaxy: M33 is the third-largest member of the Local Group, spinning majestically with 40 billion stars.
Gravitational Bound: All galaxies in the Local Group are bound together by mutual gravity, isolated from other distant clusters by vast cosmic voids.
Dark Matter Dominance: Visible stars account for less than 5% of the total mass of the Local Group; the rest is invisible dark matter.

title: The Laniakea Supercluster
Rivers of 100,000 galaxies flowing together toward a massive gravitational basin.
exponent: 520 million light-years across · Home to the Great Attractor
Laniakea Meaning: Named 'Immeasurable Heaven' in Hawaiian, this colossal supercluster defines our home galaxy cluster's broader basin of attraction.
The Great Attractor: All 100,000 galaxies in Laniakea—including our own—are inexorably sliding along gravitational streamlines toward a titanic gravitational anomaly millions of light-years away.
Supercluster Boundaries: Laniakea spans over 520 million light-years, bordering adjacent superclusters like Perseus-Pisces and Coma.
Cosmic Flow: Galaxies within Laniakea do not move randomly; they follow massive gravitational rivers streaming through the cosmos.
Mapping the Void: Laniakea was mapped using peculiar velocities—measuring how galaxy speeds deviate from the smooth expansion of the universe.

title: The Cosmic Web
Galaxies strung together like fragile glowing webs.
exponent: 1 billion light-years across
Cosmic Neural Network: Galaxies are distributed in vast intersecting filaments and clusters, resembling a colossal neural network across space.
Cosmic Voids: Spanning between these glowing filaments are immense dark voids—empty regions hundreds of millions of light-years across devoid of galaxies.
Dark Matter Scaffolding: The visible glowing web of galaxies is merely the frosting on an invisible scaffolding of primordial dark matter.
Filament Intersections: Where cosmic filaments intersect lie rich superclusters containing thousands of galaxies bound together.
Acoustic Relics: The colossal honeycomb pattern of the cosmic web was shaped by sound waves echoing through the primordial plasma of the early universe.

title: The Observable Universe
~2 trillion galaxies (conservative estimate). Beyond lies the infinite unknown.
exponent: We only see what light has reached. Beyond, realms exist in eternal shadow.
Galaxy Count: Deep field observations by Hubble and James Webb estimate there are over 2 trillion galaxies in the observable universe.
Cosmic Microwave Background: The oldest light in existence—a relic glow from the Big Bang 13.8 billion years ago—blankets every inch of the sky.
Superluminal Expansion: Space itself is expanding faster than the speed of light, meaning the most distant galaxies are permanently receding beyond our horizon.
Observable Diameter: The observable universe is roughly 93 billion light-years across despite being only 13.8 billion years old due to space expansion.
Isotropic Sky: Looking in any direction across the observable universe reveals roughly the same average distribution of galaxies and background radiation.
Stellar Count: There are more stars in the observable universe than grains of sand on all of Earth's beaches combined (estimated at 10²² stars).

title: Beyond the Observable Universe
Where light has never touched, and space stretches into the infinite.
exponent: An endless tapestry beyond our cosmic light horizon

The Light Horizon: Because light has only had 13.8 billion years to travel to us, everything beyond 46.5 billion light-years remains forever cloaked in darkness—not because nothing is there, but because light hasn't had time to arrive.
Infinite Inflation: Modern cosmological theory indicates space beyond our horizon does not end; it stretches infinitely, potentially forming an endless multiverse of disconnected pocket universes.
Causality Barrier: Space itself expands faster than light outside our horizon, creating an absolute cosmic curtain that permanently isolates our universe from whatever lies beyond.
Multiverse Possibilities: In an infinite expanding space, identical pocket universes and alternative histories repeat infinitely across the quantum landscape.
